node_sequence.text: By history, clinical examination, or laboratory findings, are there signs and symptoms suggesting delirium due to an acute physical condition or medication side effects?
Are there other explanations for the symptoms such as dementia, depression, drug or alcohol intoxication or withdrawal?
Does the person present with acute agitation and/or acute aggression?
Is the person having an acute manic episode (e.g., elevated or irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, increased activity, impulsive behaviours lasting at least 1 week)?
Is there an imminent risk of suicide?
Assess and manage imminent risk of suicide before continuing.
Has the person attempted a medically serious act of self-harm? (Check for signs of poisoning/intoxication, bleeding from self-inflicted wound, loss of consciousness, or extreme lethargy)

Is there an imminent risk of self-harm/suicide? (Current thoughts/plan of self-harm/suicide, or history of thoughts/plan in the past month or act in the past year in a person who is now extremely agitated, violent, distressed or lacks communication)
IMMINENT RISK OF SELF-HARM/SUICIDE is likely.

PROTOCOL 2: Imminent risk of self-harm/suicide. Remove means of self-harm/suicide. Create a secure environment and DO NOT leave the person alone. Supervise to ensure safety at all times. Attend to mental state. Provide psychoeducation, psychosocial, and carers support. Follow-up: maintain regular contact, decrease contact as person improves, or increase intensity and refer if not improving.
Does the person have concurrent MNS conditions? (Depression, Disorders due to substance use, Child & adolescent mental and behavioral disorders, Psychoses, Epilepsy)
Manage the concurrent conditions. See relevant modules.
Does the person have chronic pain?

Does the person have emotional symptoms severe enough to warrant clinical management? (Difficulty carrying out usual activities, repeated self-medication for emotional distress, unexplained physical symptoms, marked distress or repeated help-seeking)

Follow-up for as long as the risk of self-harm/suicide persists. Maintain regular contact. Assess for improvement; decrease contact as the person improves, or increase intensity/duration and refer to specialist if not improving.
End of Self-Harm / Suicide Assessment and Management.

cases.user_story:
Twenty-six-year-old Tasmia Rahman teaches English at a girls’ madrasa in Beanibazar, Sylhet, and lives with her parents and younger brother above their family’s stationery shop. Until recently she was known as careful and modest, keeping lesson plans neatly filed and helping her mother after Maghrib prayer. Over the last nine days, however, her family says she has slept only one or two hours a night yet wakes “full of electricity,” rearranging the shop at dawn, calling relatives with grand plans to open five branches, and spending nearly all her savings on microphones and banners for a “national education movement.” She talks rapidly, jumps from one idea to another, and insists Allah has chosen her to “correct the whole country,” but in the clinic she remains seated, answers questions, and does not threaten or hit anyone.

Her father brought her to the upazila health complex after she whispered that she must drink pesticide before Fajr so her family would be spared from a coming disaster. A bottle of insecticide is kept in the storeroom for the paddy field, and she had asked her brother where the key was. She has not swallowed anything, cut herself, hanged herself, lost consciousness, or become drowsy; examination shows no bleeding, no smell of poison, and she is alert. She is currently clear that she still intends to die “tonight if they let me,” and becomes tearful only when her mother says the pesticide has been removed.

There is no fever, head injury, seizure, dehydration, recent infection, or new medicine; her pulse, blood pressure, glucose, and basic examination are unremarkable, and she is oriented to date, place, and family members. She has no history of gradual memory loss or decline in daily skills, and she does not drink alcohol, take yaba, cannabis, sedatives, or cough syrup; her family reports no signs of intoxication or withdrawal. Before this week she was not persistently sad, slowed, hopeless, or unable to enjoy teaching, and she had not been repeatedly visiting doctors for unexplained bodily complaints or taking medicines to calm herself.

Tasmia has no chronic back, joint, abdominal, or headache pain and normally carries water, teaches classes, and helps in the shop without limitation. Her current risk is tied to the manic state with grandiose and religious delusional beliefs, making her family fearful to leave her alone even for a few minutes.
